q: Fructose, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, has its carbonyl group on carbon 2. Fructose is classified as a(n)
h: Aldose or ketose depends on where the C=O is; the suffix depends on the number of carbons.
w: A C=O on C2 (not the end) makes a ketone, and six carbons make a hexose: ketohexose. Glucose and galactose are aldohexoses.
x: An aldose has its C=O at the end of the chain, on carbon 1, as an aldehyde. Fructose's C=O is on carbon 2, inside the chain.
The "pent-" part means five carbons, but fructose has six carbons (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>).
This gets both parts wrong: a C=O on carbon 2 is not an aldehyde, and fructose has six carbons, not five.

q: In the Haworth projection of α-D-glucose, the –OH group on carbon 1 is
c: below the ring, opposite the CH<sub>2</sub>OH group
above the ring, on the same side as the CH<sub>2</sub>OH group
in the plane of the ring
h: Compare the anomeric –OH to the CH<sub>2</sub>OH on carbon 5: α is “trans,” β is “cis.”
w: In a D-sugar the CH2OH points up; in the α anomer the C1 –OH points down, opposite it. The β anomer has the C1 –OH up.
x: An –OH on the same side as the CH<sub>2</sub>OH group describes the β anomer. Recall which anomer is "trans" and which is "cis."
In a Haworth projection, groups on ring carbons are drawn above or below the ring, not in its plane.
The ring oxygen comes from the C5 –OH, not the C1 –OH. Carbon 1 keeps an –OH after the ring closes.

q: When pure α-D-glucose is dissolved in water, the solution soon contains α-D-glucose, β-D-glucose and a little open-chain glucose. This process is called
h: The ring opens at the hemiacetal and closes again with the –OH on either side.
w: Interconversion of the α and β anomers through the open-chain form is mutarotation; no bonds to other molecules are broken, so it is not hydrolysis.
x: Hydrolysis uses water to break a bond between two units, such as a glycosidic bond. Here a single glucose ring just opens and recloses.
Fermentation is the conversion of glucose to ethanol and CO<sub>2</sub> by yeast. The glucose here stays glucose; only its C1 –OH changes position.
The solution still contains only glucose forms. Nothing here changes the aldose into a ketose; only the anomeric –OH flips between up and down.

q: D-Galactose differs from D-glucose only in the position of the –OH group on carbon
h: Glucose and galactose are epimers: they differ at just one chiral carbon.
w: Galactose is the C-4 epimer of glucose. Changing C2 gives mannose; changing C5 would change D to L.
x: Changing the –OH on carbon 2 of glucose gives mannose, not galactose.
Glucose and galactose do not differ at carbon 3. Compare the Fischer projections one carbon lower down the chain.
Carbon 5 sets D or L, and both sugars here are D. Flipping C5 would change the D/L label, not turn glucose into galactose.

q: Which sugar is NOT a reducing sugar?
h: A reducing sugar needs a free hemiacetal (a ring that can open to give an aldehyde).
w: In sucrose, both anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond, so it cannot open and gives a negative Benedict's test. Maltose, lactose and glucose are reducing.
x: Maltose still has one glucose with a free hemiacetal C1, so its ring can open to an aldehyde. That makes it a reducing sugar.
In lactose, the glucose unit keeps a free hemiacetal at C1, so the ring can open and react in Benedict's test. Lactose is reducing.
Free glucose is a hemiacetal that opens to an aldehyde, so it gives a positive Benedict's test. It is a reducing sugar.

q: A patient with lactose intolerance lacks enough lactase, the enzyme that hydrolyzes lactose into
h: Lactose is milk sugar; recall which two monosaccharides it is built from.
w: Lactose → galactose + glucose. Two glucose units come from maltose; glucose + fructose comes from sucrose.
x: Two glucose units are what maltase releases from maltose. Milk sugar contains a different monosaccharide alongside glucose.
Glucose and fructose come from sucrose (table sugar) when sucrase acts on it, not from milk sugar.
Fructose is not part of lactose. Only one of these two sugars is in milk sugar; the other partner is glucose.

q: Which carbohydrate consists of exactly two glucose units joined by an α(1→4)-glycosidic bond?
h: Malt sugar comes from the breakdown of starch.
w: Starch digestion produces maltose, glucose–α(1→4)–glucose. Lactose is galactose–β(1→4)–glucose, sucrose contains fructose, and amylose is a long chain of many glucose units.
x: Lactose is a disaccharide, but it contains galactose and its bond is β(1→4), not α(1→4) between two glucose units.
Sucrose contains a fructose unit, and its linkage is α,β(1→2), not α(1→4).
Amylose does use α(1→4) bonds, but it is a long polymer of many glucose units, not exactly two.

q: In sucrose, glucose and fructose are joined by which glycosidic bond?
h: The bond connects the anomeric carbon of glucose with the anomeric carbon of fructose.
w: C1 of α-glucose bonds to C2 of β-fructose: an α,β(1→2) linkage. Because both anomeric carbons are used, sucrose is not a reducing sugar.
x: α(1→4) joins C1 of one glucose to C4 of another, as in maltose. In sucrose the bond involves the anomeric carbon of fructose, which is C2.
β(1→4) is the lactose and cellulose linkage. Sucrose's bond connects the anomeric carbon of each sugar, and fructose's anomeric carbon is not C4.
This gets the α,β part right, but carbon 4 of fructose is not its anomeric carbon. Which carbon held fructose's C=O?

q: Humans can digest starch but not cellulose because cellulose contains
c: fructose units in place of glucose units
galactose units in place of glucose units
h: Both are polymers of glucose; what differs is the linkage between units.
w: Cellulose is glucose joined by β(1→4) bonds, and human amylases hydrolyze only α bonds. Starch also has α(1→6) branches, so branching is not the difference; cellulose passes through as dietary fiber.
x: Cellulose is made only of glucose, just like starch. The difference lies in how the glucose units are linked.
α(1→6) branch points are found in starch (amylopectin) and glycogen, which we digest. Cellulose is unbranched.
Cellulose contains no galactose; it is a polymer of glucose only, just like starch.

q: Which statement best describes glycogen?
c: a highly branched glucose polymer stored in liver and muscle
an unbranched glucose polymer stored in plants
a polymer of fructose stored in the liver
a structural polymer of β-glucose in plant cell walls
h: Glycogen is “animal starch.” Think about how often it branches and where it is stored.
w: Glycogen is α(1→4)-linked glucose with frequent α(1→6) branches, making it highly branched, stored in liver and muscle. Unbranched amylose is a plant starch; cellulose is the β structural polymer.
x: That describes amylose, the unbranched plant starch. Glycogen is the animal storage form and has many branch points.
Glycogen is built from glucose, not fructose, and it is stored in muscle as well as liver.
That describes cellulose, the β-linked structural polymer of plants. Glycogen is an animal energy-storage polymer with α linkages.

q: For an aldohexose drawn as a Fischer projection, which carbon's –OH position determines whether the sugar is D or L?
h: Look at the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl group.
w: C5 is the chiral carbon farthest from the C=O, so carbon 5 decides: an –OH on the right makes it D. C1 and C6 are not chiral at all.
x: Carbon 1 is the aldehyde carbon (–CHO). It is not a chiral carbon, so it has no –OH position to compare.
Carbon 2 is chiral, but it is the chiral carbon closest to the C=O. D/L is set by the one farthest from it.
Carbon 6 is a –CH<sub>2</sub>OH group with two H atoms, so it is not chiral and cannot set D or L.

q: When glucose forms its six-membered ring, the –OH on carbon 5 adds to the carbonyl group on carbon 1. The ring is a cyclic
h: An alcohol adding once to an aldehyde gives which group?
w: One alcohol (the C5 –OH) adding to an aldehyde (C1) forms a hemiacetal. A glycosidic bond to a second sugar turns it into an acetal. A hemiketal would form from a ketone sugar such as fructose.
x: An acetal forms when a second alcohol (–OR) adds, as in a glycosidic bond. Ring closure adds only one alcohol to the aldehyde.
An ester forms from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. Glucose's C1 is an aldehyde, not a carboxylic acid.
A hemiketal forms when an alcohol adds to a ketone, as in fructose. Glucose's carbon 1 is an aldehyde carbon.

q: In the five-membered ring form of fructose, the anomeric carbon (the one whose –OH can be α or β) is carbon
h: The anomeric carbon is the former carbonyl carbon. Where is the C=O in fructose?
w: Fructose's C=O is on C2, so after cyclization C2 is the anomeric carbon. C1 is the anomeric carbon only in aldoses such as glucose.
x: Carbon 1 is the anomeric carbon in aldoses like glucose. In fructose, C1 is a –CH<sub>2</sub>OH group outside the ring.
In the five-membered ring, the C5 –OH supplies the ring oxygen. C5 is where the ring closes from, not the former carbonyl carbon.
Carbon 6 is a –CH<sub>2</sub>OH group outside the ring; it is not chiral. Look for the carbon that was the C=O carbon.

q: Type B red blood cells carry an extra galactose unit on their surface markers that type O cells lack; type A cells carry an extra amino sugar (N-acetylgalactosamine) instead. The ABO blood types therefore differ in the
c: carbohydrate chains attached to the surface of red blood cells
number of hemoglobin molecules inside each red blood cell
fatty acids in the phospholipids of the red cell membrane
amount of iron in the heme groups of the red blood cells
h: Antibodies recognize “identity tags” on the outer surface of the red cell membrane. Which class of biomolecule forms these surface markers?
w: All red cells carry a basic oligosaccharide (type O). Type A adds N-acetylgalactosamine, type B adds galactose, and type AB has both. So the blood types differ in the carbohydrate chains on the red blood cell surface, which is why mismatched transfusions trigger antibodies.
x: Hemoglobin is inside the cell, where antibodies cannot reach it. Blood type markers sit on the outer surface of the membrane.
The question describes extra galactose and an amino sugar on the markers. Those are not fatty acids.
Heme iron is inside the cell and is the same in all blood types. The extra units named in the question are sugars on the cell surface.

q: Which pair of polysaccharides contains α(1→6)-glycosidic bonds at branch points?
h: Unbranched chains have only one kind of glycosidic bond. Which two glucose polymers are branched?
w: All three starch-type polymers have α(1→4) chains, but only amylopectin (branch about every 25 units) and glycogen (about every 10 units) also have α(1→6) branch points. Amylose is unbranched α(1→4); cellulose is unbranched β(1→4).
x: Neither is branched: amylose is unbranched α(1→4) glucose, and cellulose is unbranched β(1→4) glucose.
Amylopectin is branched, but amylose is an unbranched α(1→4) chain with no α(1→6) bonds.
Glycogen is branched, but cellulose is an unbranched β(1→4) chain with no α(1→6) bonds.

q: An infant with galactosemia cannot convert galactose into glucose, so toxic galactose products build up. Which food must be removed from the infant's diet?
c: table sugar, because sucrose contains galactose
h: Which disaccharide is made of galactose + glucose, and where is it found?
w: Lactose (milk sugar) is galactose + glucose, so milk and other lactose-containing foods must be removed. Sucrose is glucose + fructose, and starch contains only glucose.
x: Sucrose is glucose + fructose; it contains no galactose, so table sugar is not the problem here.
Starch is built only from glucose units, so bread starch does not supply galactose.
Fructose is a monosaccharide on its own; it does not contain galactose. Look for the disaccharide that does.

q: In poorly controlled diabetes, excess glucose in the lens of the eye is converted to sorbitol, which contributes to cataracts. Sorbitol is
c: a sugar alcohol formed by reducing the aldehyde of glucose
a carboxylic acid formed by oxidizing the aldehyde of glucose
a disaccharide formed by joining two glucose molecules
a ketose formed by moving the carbonyl of glucose to C2
h: The name ends in -ol. What happens to an aldehyde group when it is reduced?
w: Reduction of the aldehyde (–CHO) on C1 of glucose gives a primary alcohol (–CH2OH), so sorbitol (glucitol) is a sugar alcohol. Oxidizing the aldehyde would give gluconic acid, a carboxylic acid. Sorbitol is also used as a sugar-free sweetener.
x: Oxidizing the aldehyde gives gluconic acid, a carboxylic acid. The "-ol" ending of sorbitol points to the opposite kind of reaction.
Sorbitol comes from a single glucose molecule; no glycosidic bond is formed. Joining two glucose units would give a disaccharide such as maltose.
Moving the C=O to C2 would give fructose, which still has a carbonyl. The "-ol" ending tells you sorbitol has no C=O left.

q: Ribulose, an intermediate in photosynthesis and the pentose phosphate pathway, has the open-chain structure CH<sub>2</sub>OH–CO–CHOH–CHOH–CH<sub>2</sub>OH. How is ribulose classified?
h: Count the carbons for the ending, then decide whether the C=O is at the end of the chain (aldehyde) or inside it (ketone).
w: Ribulose has 5 carbons (pentose) and its C=O is on carbon 2, inside the chain, so it is a ketone: ketopentose. An aldopentose (like ribose) has the C=O on carbon 1 as –CHO.
x: An aldopentose (like ribose) has a –CHO on carbon 1. Here carbon 1 is CH<sub>2</sub>OH and the C=O is on carbon 2.
Count the carbons in CH<sub>2</sub>OH–CO–CHOH–CHOH–CH<sub>2</sub>OH again: there are five, not six.
A tetrose has four carbons, and "aldo" means a –CHO at the end. This chain has five carbons and its C=O is inside the chain.

q: D-Glucose cyclizes to form β-D-glucopyranose, a six-membered ring. How many chiral carbons does β-D-glucopyranose have?
h: Open-chain glucose has chiral carbons C2–C5. What happens to the carbonyl carbon C1 when it becomes the hemiacetal carbon?
w: Open-chain glucose has 4 chiral carbons (C2–C5). On ring closure, C1 becomes a hemiacetal carbon bonded to –OH, –O– (ring), –H and C2: four different groups, so it is a new chiral center. Total: 5. C6 (–CH2OH) is never chiral.
x: 4 is the count for open-chain glucose (C2–C5). Ring closure turns C1 into a carbon with four different groups.
6 counts every carbon, but C6 is a –CH<sub>2</sub>OH with two H atoms, so it is not chiral.
3 leaves out some of C2–C5, which are all chiral in glucose, and also misses the new center at C1.

q: In lactose (milk sugar), carbon 1 of β-D-galactose is bonded through an oxygen atom to carbon 4 of D-glucose. How is this glycosidic linkage labeled?
h: Name the linkage with the anomeric form of the first sugar, then the two carbon numbers that are joined.
w: The anomeric carbon (C1) of galactose is in the β form and is joined to C4 of glucose, so the linkage is β(1→4). Lactase must break this β bond; α(1→4) is the linkage in maltose and starch.
x: α would mean the galactose C1 bond is in the α form, as in maltose. The question tells you galactose is in the β form.
The β part is right, but the question says galactose bonds to carbon 4 of glucose, not carbon 6.
Check both parts: the galactose is in the β form, and it is bonded to carbon 4 of glucose.

q: Maltose is two glucose units joined by an α(1→4) linkage. Which statement correctly describes carbon 1 of each glucose unit in maltose?
c: The linked C1 is an acetal; the other C1 is a hemiacetal
Both C1 carbons are acetals, so maltose is not reducing
Both C1 carbons are hemiacetals, held by an ester bond
The linked C1 is a hemiacetal; the other C1 is an acetal
h: A hemiacetal carbon has one –OH and one –OR; an acetal carbon has two –OR groups. Which C1 is tied up in the glycosidic bond?
w: C1 of the first glucose bears the ring O and the glycosidic O (two –OR groups): an acetal. C1 of the second glucose still has a free –OH and the ring O: a hemiacetal, which can open to an aldehyde, so maltose is a reducing sugar.
x: Only one C1 is used in the α(1→4) bond. The second glucose's C1 keeps its –OH, so maltose is a reducing sugar.
A glycosidic bond is an ether-type C–O–C link, not an ester. Also, the C1 in the glycosidic bond carries two –OR groups, not one.
This has the two C1 carbons reversed. The C1 in the glycosidic bond carries two –OR groups; which C1 still has a free –OH?

q: How is the enantiomer of D-glucose drawn in a Fischer projection?
c: L-glucose: the –OH on all chiral carbons is moved to the opposite side
L-glucose: only the –OH on carbon 5 is moved to the opposite side
β-D-glucose: only the –OH on carbon 1 is moved to the opposite side
D-galactose: only the –OH on carbon 4 is moved to the opposite side
h: Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images. In a mirror image, which chiral centers are inverted?
w: An enantiomer is the mirror image, so all four chiral centers (C2–C5) are reversed, giving L-glucose. Flipping only C5 gives a different sugar (a diastereomer, not glucose); flipping only C4 gives galactose, an epimer.
x: Flipping only C5 changes the D/L label, but the result is not the mirror image of glucose; it is a different sugar (a diastereomer).
α and β anomers differ only at C1 of the ring form; they are not mirror images. An enantiomer is a full mirror image.
Flipping only C4 gives galactose, an epimer of glucose. A mirror image must reverse more than one chiral center.

q: α-D-Glucose and β-D-glucose are called anomers because they differ only in
c: the position of the –OH on the hemiacetal carbon, C1
the position of the –OH on carbon 5, which sets D or L
the position of the –OH on carbon 4 of the ring
the size of the ring, five-membered versus six-membered
h: Anomers form when the ring closes. Which carbon becomes the new chiral center during cyclization?
w: Ring closure makes C1 (the anomeric carbon) a new chiral center, so the –OH there can be down (α) or up (β): anomers differ only at C1. Differing only at C4 makes epimers such as glucose and galactose.
x: Both α-D- and β-D-glucose are D sugars, so their C5 –OH is the same. Anomers differ at the carbon that becomes chiral when the ring closes.
Sugars that differ only at C4 are epimers, like glucose and galactose. Anomers differ at a different carbon.
α- and β-D-glucose here are both six-membered rings. Anomers have the same ring size and differ at one specific carbon.

q: Amylose, amylopectin, glycogen and cellulose are all hydrolyzed completely to which monosaccharide?
h: These four polysaccharides differ in their linkages and branching, not in their building block.
w: All four are polymers of glucose only; they differ in α versus β linkages and branching. Glucose + fructose make sucrose, and glucose + galactose make lactose.
x: Glucose + fructose is what sucrose gives on hydrolysis. None of these four polysaccharides contains fructose.
Glucose + galactose is what lactose gives on hydrolysis. These four polysaccharides contain no galactose.
These polymers contain no fructose. They differ in linkages and branching, not in their building block.

q: A dietitian notes that table sugar dissolves easily in water, but cooking oil does not. Which statement best explains why most simple carbohydrates are water soluble?
c: Their many –OH groups form hydrogen bonds with water
Their glycosidic bonds ionize to form charged ions in water
Their long hydrocarbon chains attract water molecules
Their ester groups are hydrolyzed by water as they dissolve
h: Look for groups that contain O–H. What intermolecular force can they form with water?
w: Sugars carry many polar –OH groups that hydrogen bond with water, so they dissolve. Lipids are mostly long nonpolar hydrocarbon chains with few H-bonding groups, so they are insoluble. Glycosidic bonds do not ionize.
x: Glycosidic bonds are covalent C–O–C bonds; they do not ionize in water. Look for polar groups that interact with water.
Long hydrocarbon chains are nonpolar and repel water; that describes oils, not sugars.
Simple sugars do not contain ester groups, and dissolving is a physical change, not a hydrolysis reaction.

q: Sucrase, an enzyme on the lining of the small intestine, hydrolyzes table sugar. Which monosaccharides are absorbed as a result?
h: Name the two monosaccharides that make up sucrose.
w: Sucrose is glucose bonded to fructose, so its hydrolysis gives glucose and fructose. Glucose + galactose come from lactose (lactase), and two glucose units come from maltose (maltase).
x: Glucose and galactose come from lactose (milk sugar), digested by lactase. Table sugar has a different partner for glucose.
Two glucose units come from maltose, digested by maltase. Sucrose contains only one glucose unit.
Galactose is not part of sucrose; it comes from milk sugar. Recall the two sugars that make up table sugar.

q: An aldohexose is drawn as a Fischer projection. Reading from C2 down to C5, its –OH groups point right, left, left, right. Which sugar is it?
h: Start from D-glucose (right, left, right, right). Find which carbon is different, then use the last chiral carbon (C5) for D or L.
w: D-glucose is right, left, right, right. This sugar differs only at C4, which makes it galactose, and the –OH on C5 points right, so it is D-galactose. L-galactose would have every –OH reversed, not just one.
x: In L-galactose every –OH is reversed. Here the bottom chiral carbon (C5) has its –OH on the right, which means D.
D-mannose differs from D-glucose at C2 (left, left, right, right). Here C2 points right, just as in glucose.
D-glucose is right, left, right, right. Compare carbon by carbon: one position here is different.

q: In the Fischer projection of D-mannose, the –OH groups on C2, C3, C4 and C5 point left, left, right, right. How are these –OH groups drawn in L-mannose?
h: L-mannose is the enantiomer (mirror image) of D-mannose. What happens to every chiral carbon in a mirror image?
w: Enantiomers are mirror images, so every chiral –OH switches sides: left, left, right, right → right, right, left, left. Flipping only C5 (left, left, right, left) gives a different sugar (a diastereomer), not the enantiomer.
x: This flips only C5. That changes the D/L label but gives a different sugar, not the mirror image of D-mannose.
This flips C2, C3 and C4 but leaves C5 on the right. A mirror image reverses every chiral carbon, including C5.
This is the same pattern as D-mannose itself, so nothing has been mirrored. An enantiomer has every –OH on the opposite side.

q: D-Ribose is an aldopentose. How many chiral carbons does its open-chain form have, and how many stereoisomers (2<sup>n</sup>) are possible for an aldopentose?
h: The aldehyde carbon (C1) and the end CH<sub>2</sub>OH carbon are not chiral. Count only carbons with H and OH on the sides.
w: C1 (–CHO) and C5 (–CH2OH) are not chiral, so C2, C3 and C4 are: n = 3, and 23 = 8 stereoisomers (3 chiral carbons). Counting all 5 carbons as chiral is the common mistake.
x: 4 chiral carbons and 16 stereoisomers fit an aldohexose. Ribose has only five carbons, and its ends are not chiral.
The chiral count is right, but stereoisomers = 2<sup>n</sup>, not 2 × n. Recalculate 2<sup>3</sup>.
This counts all five carbons as chiral. C1 (–CHO) and C5 (–CH<sub>2</sub>OH) do not have four different groups.

q: Dihydroxyacetone, HOCH<sub>2</sub>–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>OH, is the active ingredient in sunless tanning lotions. How is it classified?
h: Count the carbons for the size, then decide whether the C=O is an aldehyde (end carbon) or a ketone (middle carbon).
w: It has 3 carbons (triose), and the C=O is on the middle carbon, so it is a ketone: a ketotriose. Its isomer glyceraldehyde, with –CHO at C1, is the aldotriose.
x: An aldotriose (glyceraldehyde) has –CHO on an end carbon. In HOCH<sub>2</sub>–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>OH the C=O is on the middle carbon.
Count the carbons in HOCH<sub>2</sub>–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>OH: there are three, not four.
Count the carbons in HOCH<sub>2</sub>–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>OH again: there are three, not five.

q: Compare open-chain D-glucose with D-mannose: same formula, but the C2 –OH points left in mannose and right in glucose, with C3–C5 identical. What is the relationship?
h: Compare the chiral carbons. How many are different, and are the sugars mirror images?
w: Stereoisomers that differ at only one chiral carbon are epimers. Enantiomers differ at every chiral carbon; anomers differ only at the anomeric carbon of a ring (C1), not at C2 of the open chain.
x: Enantiomers are mirror images that differ at every chiral carbon. Here C3–C5 are identical, so they are not mirror images.
Anomers differ at the anomeric carbon (C1) of a ring form. These are open-chain sugars that differ at C2.
Structural isomers have atoms connected in a different order. Here the connections are identical; only the 3-D arrangement at one carbon differs.

q: A Haworth projection of a D-hexopyranose shows the –OH on C1 pointing up, the –OH on C2 pointing down, the –OH on C3 pointing up and the –OH on C4 pointing up. Which sugar is it?
h: Anomeric –OH up = β, down = α (for D-sugars). D-glucose in a Haworth ring has C2 down, C3 up, C4 down. Which carbon is different?
w: The C1 –OH is up, so it is β. Glucose has its C4 –OH down; here C4 is up, so it is galactose (the C4 epimer): β-D-galactose. Calling it glucose misses the C4 difference.
x: For a D-sugar, an anomeric –OH pointing down is α. Here the C1 –OH points up.
In β-D-glucose the C4 –OH points down. Here the C4 –OH points up, so this is not glucose.
Check two things: the C1 –OH points up here (not the α position), and the C4 –OH points up, which does not match glucose.

q: A food-science student heats four sugar solutions with Benedict's reagent (blue Cu<sup>2+</sup>). Which solution forms an orange-red precipitate?
h: Benedict's reagent is reduced only by sugars with a free aldehyde or a hemiacetal that can open to one.
w: Lactose keeps a free hemiacetal on its glucose unit, so it reduces Cu2+ to Cu2O. Sucrose has both anomeric carbons tied up; sorbitol has no carbonyl; gluconic acid is already oxidized.
x: In sucrose both anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond, so no ring can open to an aldehyde. It gives no precipitate.
Sorbitol is a sugar alcohol with no aldehyde or hemiacetal, so it cannot reduce Cu<sup>2+</sup>.
Gluconic acid's C1 is already oxidized to –COOH, so there is no aldehyde left to reduce Cu<sup>2+</sup>.

q: When D-galactose reacts with a mild oxidizing agent, its –CHO group is oxidized. What is the product?
h: Oxidizing an aldehyde gives a carboxylic acid; the sugar name changes to an '-onic acid'.
w: The –CHO on C1 becomes –COOH, giving D-galactonic acid. D-galactitol (an '-itol' sugar alcohol) is the product of reduction, not oxidation.
x: An "-itol" name is a sugar alcohol, which forms by reduction of the –CHO, not oxidation.
Gluconic acid comes from oxidizing glucose. Oxidation changes C1 only, so the product keeps the parent sugar's name.
Lactic acid is a three-carbon product of anaerobic glucose breakdown. Mild oxidation changes only the –CHO of the six-carbon sugar.

q: Isomaltose, a product of starch digestion at the branch points, joins two glucose units: the α anomeric carbon of one unit links via –O– to C6 of the other. Which label describes this bond?
h: The label gives the anomer (α or β) of the sugar using its anomeric carbon, then the two carbon numbers joined.
w: The first glucose uses its α anomeric carbon (C1), and it joins C6 of the next unit: α(1→6), the same link found at the branch points of amylopectin and glycogen.
x: The question says the linking anomeric carbon is in the α form, so a β label does not fit.
α(1→4) joins C1 to C4, as in maltose and the straight parts of starch. Here the bond goes to C6 of the other unit.
β(1→4) is the cellulose and lactose linkage. Here the anomeric carbon is α and it links to C6.

q: In sucrose, C1 of glucose and C2 of fructose are both used in the glycosidic bond. Which functional groups are present at these two anomeric carbons?
c: an acetal at glucose C1 and a ketal at fructose C2
a hemiacetal at glucose C1 and a hemiketal at fructose C2
a hemiacetal at glucose C1 and a ketal at fructose C2
a ketal at glucose C1 and an acetal at fructose C2
h: An anomeric carbon with –OR and –O– (ring) is a full acetal/ketal; one with –OH and –O– is a hemi-. Glucose came from an aldehyde, fructose from a ketone.
w: Both anomeric carbons carry two –O–R groups and no free –OH, so neither is 'hemi'. Glucose C1 (from an aldehyde) is an acetal, fructose C2 (from a ketone) is a ketal. With no hemiacetal left, sucrose is not a reducing sugar.
x: A "hemi-" carbon still has a free –OH. In sucrose both anomeric carbons are used in the glycosidic bond, so neither has an –OH left.
Glucose C1 is part of the glycosidic bond, so it has no free –OH. A hemiacetal there would make sucrose a reducing sugar.
The labels are swapped. Acetal goes with a carbon that came from an aldehyde, and ketal with one that came from a ketone.

q: Salivary amylase begins hydrolyzing the amylose in a cracker while it is being chewed. Which disaccharide is a major product?
h: Amylose is a chain of glucose units with α(1→4) bonds. Which disaccharide is two glucose units with that same linkage?
w: Breaking amylose's α(1→4) chain into two-glucose pieces gives maltose (glucose–α(1→4)–glucose). Lactose and sucrose contain galactose or fructose; cellobiose has a β(1→4) bond, like cellulose.
x: Lactose contains galactose, which is not part of amylose. Amylose is built only from glucose.
Sucrose contains fructose, which is not part of amylose. Amylose is built only from glucose.
Cellobiose is two glucose units joined β(1→4), the repeat unit of cellulose. Amylose has α(1→4) bonds.

q: Sucrose is completely hydrolyzed by the enzyme sucrase. How many grams of glucose are produced from 34.2 g of sucrose?
h: Write the hydrolysis: sucrose + H<sub>2</sub>O → ? Find moles of sucrose, then use the mole ratio to glucose.
w: Sucrose + H2O → glucose + fructose, a 1 : 1 ratio. 34.2 g ÷ 342.3 g mol⁻¹ = 0.0999 mol sucrose → 0.0999 mol glucose × 180.16 g mol⁻¹ = 18.0 g. 36.0 g assumes two glucose per sucrose, which is true for maltose, not sucrose.
x: 36.0 g assumes two glucose per sucrose. That is true for maltose; sucrose gives one glucose and one fructose.
34.2 g is the mass of sucrose you started with. Convert to moles and use the mole ratio to glucose.
9.00 g is half the expected amount, as if only half a glucose formed per sucrose. Check the 1 : 1 ratio in the hydrolysis equation.

q: Is the aldohexose shown a D-sugar or an L-sugar, and why?
c: L, because the –OH on C5 points to the left
D, because the –OH on C2 points to the right
D, because the –OH on C4 points to the right
L, because the –OH on C3 points to the right
h: Find the chiral carbon farthest from the C=O (just above the bottom CH<sub>2</sub>OH).
w: D or L is decided only by the bottom chiral carbon (C5 in a hexose). Here its –OH is on the left, so this is an L-sugar (it is L-galactose). The C2, C3 and C4 positions do not decide D or L.
x: Look again: the C2 –OH points left. In any case, C2 does not decide D or L; only the bottom chiral carbon does.
The C4 –OH does point right, but C4 does not decide D or L. Check the chiral carbon just above the CH<sub>2</sub>OH.
L is the right label, but C3 is not the reason. D or L is decided by only one chiral carbon: the one farthest from the C=O.

q: How is the monosaccharide shown classified?
h: Count every carbon, look for –CHO at the top vs. C=O inside the chain, then check the bottom chiral carbon.
w: Five carbons (pent-ose), a C=O on C2 (keto-), and the –OH on the bottom chiral carbon (C4) points right (D): a D-ketopentose (D-xylulose). Count every carbon, including both CH2OH ends: there are 5, not 6, so it is not a hexose.
x: The bottom chiral carbon (the one just above the CH<sub>2</sub>OH) has its –OH on the right. Which label does that give?
An aldose has –CHO at the top. This sugar has CH<sub>2</sub>OH at the top and the C=O on carbon 2.
Count every carbon, including both CH<sub>2</sub>OH ends and the C=O carbon. There are not six.

q: Glyceraldehyde is the reference sugar for the D/L system. How is the molecule shown classified?
h: Three carbons = triose. A –CHO at the top makes it an aldose. The –OH side on the chiral carbon gives D or L.
w: It has 3 carbons and an aldehyde (–CHO), so it is an aldotriose. The only chiral carbon has its –OH on the left, so it is L-glyceraldehyde, an L-aldotriose.
x: In this drawing the –OH on the chiral carbon points to the left. Which label does that give?
Glyceraldehyde has –CHO at the top, which is an aldehyde, not a ketone.
Both parts are off: the top carbon is –CHO (an aldehyde), and the –OH on the chiral carbon points left.

q: For the sugar shown, which description is correct?
h: Only carbons bonded to H and OH on the sides are chiral. The CHO and CH<sub>2</sub>OH carbons are not.
w: Four carbons with a –CHO: an aldotetrose. The two middle carbons each carry H, OH and two different chain groups, so there are 2 chiral carbons. The bottom chiral carbon has –OH on the right: D (D-erythrose).
x: The –CHO and –CH<sub>2</sub>OH end carbons are not chiral. Count only the carbons with H and OH on the sides.
The bottom chiral carbon has its –OH on the right. Which label does that give?
The top group is –CHO, so this is an aldose, not a ketose. Also count the chiral carbons again: the ends are not chiral.

q: Which Fischer projection shows D-glucose?
h: Recall the left/right pattern of the –OH groups on C2–C5 of D-glucose. The bottom chiral carbon must have its –OH on the right.
w: D-glucose has –OH groups right, left, right, right on C2–C5, the pattern in structure III. The mirror image (all reversed) is L-glucose; changing only C2 gives D-mannose; changing only C4 gives D-galactose.
x: Structure IV has every –OH reversed from D-glucose (left, right, left, left). Its bottom –OH points left, so it is an L-sugar.
Structure II has the C2 –OH on the left (left, left, right, right). That pattern is D-mannose.
Structure I has the C4 –OH on the left (right, left, left, right). That pattern is D-galactose.

q: Galactose is one of the two sugars released when lactase digests milk sugar (lactose). Which Fischer projection shows D-galactose?
h: D-galactose is the C4 epimer of D-glucose (right, left, right, right).
w: D-galactose differs from D-glucose only at C4: right, left, left, right, structure II. One structure is D-glucose, one is L-galactose (every –OH reversed), and one is D-talose (C2 also changed).
x: Structure III is right, left, right, right: D-glucose itself. Galactose differs from it at one carbon.
Structure I is left, right, right, left: every –OH reversed, so its bottom –OH points left. That is an L-sugar.
Structure IV is left, left, left, right. It differs from D-glucose at C2 as well as C4, so it is a different sugar (D-talose).

q: Which Fischer projection shows D-fructose, the sugar in honey and fruit?
h: Fructose is a ketohexose (C=O on C2). Its C3–C5 –OH groups match C3–C5 of D-glucose.
w: D-fructose has its C=O on C2 and –OH groups left, right, right on C3–C5 (same as C3–C5 of D-glucose): structure IV. One ketose is L-fructose (all reversed), one is D-sorbose (C3 and C4 swapped), and the aldose is D-glucose.
x: Structure III is a ketose with C3–C5 right, left, left. Every –OH is reversed, and the bottom –OH points left, so it is an L-sugar.
Structure I has –CHO at the top, so it is an aldose (D-glucose). Fructose has its C=O on C2.
Structure II is a D-ketose, but its C3–C5 pattern (right, left, right) does not match C3–C5 of D-glucose. It is D-sorbose.

q: Name the sugar shown. (D-glucose has its –OH groups right, left, right, right on C2–C5; D-mannose differs from D-glucose only at C2, and D-galactose only at C4.)
h: Compare carbon by carbon with D-glucose. Which carbon is different? Then check the bottom chiral carbon for D/L.
w: Compared with D-glucose, only the C2 –OH is moved (to the left), so this is the C2 epimer, D-mannose. The bottom –OH still points right, so it is D, not L. D-galactose would differ at C4.
x: D-galactose would differ from D-glucose at C4. Here the C4 –OH points right, just as in glucose.
The bottom chiral carbon has its –OH on the right, so this is a D-sugar, not L.
L-glucose has every –OH reversed (left, right, left, left). Here only one carbon differs from D-glucose, and the bottom –OH points right.

q: How many chiral carbons are in the open-chain sugar shown?
h: A chiral carbon has four different groups. The C=O carbon and the CH<sub>2</sub>OH carbons cannot be chiral.
w: D-fructose has 6 carbons, but C1 and C6 are CH2OH and C2 is the C=O carbon. Only C3, C4 and C5 carry four different groups: 3 chiral carbons. Answering 4 counts the C=O carbon as in an aldohexose.
x: 4 is the count for an aldohexose. Here C2 is a C=O carbon, which cannot be chiral.
5 counts too many: the two CH<sub>2</sub>OH carbons and the C=O carbon cannot have four different groups.
2 misses one. Check each carbon that carries an H and an OH on its sides.

q: How many chiral carbons are in the ring form of glucose shown?
h: Ring closure makes C1 a new chiral carbon. Check C1 through C5; C6 is a CH<sub>2</sub>OH.
w: In the open chain, glucose has 4 chiral carbons (C2–C5). Closing the ring turns C1 into the anomeric carbon with four different groups (ring O, OH, H, C2), so the ring form has 5. C6 (CH2OH) is not chiral.
x: 4 is the count for open-chain glucose. In the ring, C1 now has four different groups (ring O, OH, H and C2).
6 counts C6 as well, but C6 is a –CH<sub>2</sub>OH with two H atoms, so it is not chiral.
3 misses some ring carbons. Check C1 through C5 one at a time for four different groups.

q: The Haworth projection shows a form of D-glucose. Which anomer is it?
c: β, because the C1 –OH points up, on the same side as the CH<sub>2</sub>OH
α, because the C1 –OH points up, on the same side as the CH<sub>2</sub>OH
β, because the C2 –OH points down
α, because the C4 –OH points down
h: Look only at the anomeric carbon (C1, next to the ring O). Compare its –OH with the CH<sub>2</sub>OH on C5.
w: For D-sugars, the anomeric –OH up (cis to the CH2OH on C5) is β; down (trans) is α. Here the C1 –OH points up, so this is β-D-glucose. The –OH groups on C2–C4 do not decide α or β.
x: The C1 –OH does point up on the same side as the CH<sub>2</sub>OH, but that position is not α for a D-sugar.
β is right, but the C2 –OH does not decide α or β. Only the anomeric carbon's –OH matters.
The C4 –OH does not decide α or β. Look only at the anomeric carbon next to the ring oxygen.

q: The five-membered ring shown is a form of D-fructose. What is its full name?
h: Count the ring atoms (5 = furanose). For fructose the anomeric carbon is C2; check whether its –OH points down or up.
w: The ring has 4 C + 1 O, a furanose. At the anomeric carbon (C2) the –OH points down, opposite the CH2OH on C5, so it is α: α-D-fructofuranose. A pyranose has a six-membered ring.
x: β would need the C2 –OH on the same side as the CH<sub>2</sub>OH on C5. Check which way the C2 –OH points in this drawing.
Pyranose means a six-membered ring. Count the ring atoms here: four carbons and one oxygen.
The question says this is a form of D-fructose, and its anomeric carbon is C2, as in a ketose. Glucose is an aldose.

q: Name the sugar shown.
h: Decide α/β at C1 first. Then compare C2–C4 with glucose (C2 –OH down, C3 up, C4 down).
w: The C1 –OH is up (β). The C4 –OH points up, while glucose has it down; that single change at C4 makes this β-D-galactopyranose. Mannose would differ at C2 instead.
x: For a D-sugar, α means the C1 –OH points down. In this drawing the C1 –OH points up.
In β-D-glucose the C4 –OH points down. Compare C2–C4 here with glucose: one of them points the other way.
Mannose differs from glucose at C2 (C2 –OH up). Here the C2 –OH points down, as in glucose.

q: The ring sugar on top forms when an open-chain sugar cyclizes. Which Fischer projection (I–IV) is that open-chain sugar?
h: For a D-sugar: an –OH pointing DOWN in the Haworth ring was on the RIGHT in the Fischer projection; UP was on the LEFT.
w: In the ring, C2 –OH is up (left), C3 up (left), C4 down (right), and the CH2OH on C5 is up (a D-sugar, C5 –OH right). Left, left, right, right is D-mannose, structure IV. The anomeric C1 is the former –CHO, so α or β does not matter.
x: Structure III is right, left, right, right: D-glucose. In the ring, the C2 and C3 –OH groups both point up, so both were on the left.
Structure I has C4 and C5 –OH groups on the left, so it is an L-sugar. The CH<sub>2</sub>OH pointing up in the ring tells you it is D.
Structure II has C4 on the left (left, left, left, right). In the ring the C4 –OH points down, which means right in the Fischer projection.

q: Which open-chain sugar cyclized to form the ring shown?
h: Count the carbons (four in the ring plus the CH<sub>2</sub>OH). Check whether C2 has an –OH.
w: The ring has C1–C4 plus a CH2OH (C5): a pentose. C2 and C3 both have –OH pointing down (right in Fischer), like D-ribose (right, right, right). It has an –OH on C2, so it is D-ribose (the sugar of RNA and ATP), not deoxyribose; D-xylose would have its C3 –OH up, and fructose would carry a CH2OH on the anomeric carbon.
x: Deoxyribose has no –OH on C2 (just two H). In this ring, C2 still carries an –OH.
Fructose is a hexose, and its anomeric carbon would also carry a CH<sub>2</sub>OH. Count the carbons here: four in the ring plus one CH<sub>2</sub>OH.
D-xylose would have its C3 –OH pointing up in the ring (left in Fischer). Here both the C2 and C3 –OH groups point down.

q: Which labeled carbon is the anomeric carbon?
h: The anomeric carbon was the C=O carbon of the open chain. It is bonded to the ring O and to an –OH.
w: Carbon a (C1) is bonded to two oxygens: the ring O and the –OH. It was the aldehyde carbon before the ring closed, and its –OH sets α or β. Carbon d (C5) is also next to the ring O, but it carries the CH2OH, not a second O.
x: Carbon b (C2) carries only an H and an –OH; it is not bonded to the ring oxygen.
Carbon c (C4) carries only an H and an –OH. The anomeric carbon is bonded to two oxygens.
Carbon d (C5) is next to the ring O, but its other group is the CH<sub>2</sub>OH, not an –OH. It was not the C=O carbon.

q: In this form of fructose, which labeled atom is the anomeric carbon?
h: In a ketose, the ring closes at the former C=O carbon, C2. Look for the carbon bonded to the ring O and an –OH.
w: Fructose is a ketose: its C=O was on C2, so the anomeric carbon is C2, atom a, bonded to the ring O, an –OH and the C1 CH2OH. Atom d is the ring oxygen, not a carbon; atoms b and c (C3, C4) carry only H and OH.
x: Atom b carries only H and –OH and is not bonded to the ring oxygen. The anomeric carbon was the C=O carbon of the ketose.
Atom c carries only H and –OH. Look for the carbon bonded to both the ring O and an –OH.
Atom d is the ring oxygen, not a carbon. The anomeric carbon is one of the carbons next to it.

q: Maltose, formed when amylase digests starch, is shown. What type of glycosidic bond joins the two glucose units?
h: Find which carbon of each ring the bridging O joins. Then check whether the left ring's C1 bond to that O points down or up.
w: The bridging O joins C1 of the left glucose to C4 of the right glucose: (1→4). At C1 the bond points down, so it is α(1→4), the same bond as in starch. β(1→4) would point up, as in cellulose.
x: For β the C1 bond to the bridging O would point up. Check which way it points at C1 of the left ring.
α(1→6) would connect to the CH<sub>2</sub>OH carbon (C6) of the right ring. Here the O connects to a ring carbon.
α,β(1→2) is the sucrose bond, which joins glucose to C2 of fructose. Both rings here are glucose; check which right-ring carbon the O joins.

q: Lactose, the sugar in milk, is shown. What type of glycosidic bond joins its two rings?
h: Number the carbons from the ring O. The bridge starts at C1 of the left ring; is that bond up or down?
w: The bond leaves C1 of the left ring (galactose) pointing up (β) and reaches C4 of the right ring (glucose): a β(1→4) glycosidic bond. Lactase is the enzyme that breaks it.
x: α would mean the bond at C1 of the left ring points down. Here it points up.
(1→6) would link to the CH<sub>2</sub>OH carbon (C6). Here the bridging O attaches directly to a ring carbon of the right sugar.
α,β(1→2) is the sucrose bond to C2 of fructose. Both rings here are six-membered aldoses, and the O reaches a different carbon.

q: Sucrose (table sugar) is shown. Which glycosidic bond joins glucose (left) and fructose (right)?
h: Look at which carbon of each ring the O bridges. The fructose anomeric carbon is C2.
w: The O joins C1 of α-glucose (bond down) to C2 of β-fructose. Both anomeric carbons are used, so the link is α,β(1→2) (also written α(1→2)β).
x: α(1→4) joins two glucose units, as in maltose. Here the right ring is fructose, and the O reaches its anomeric carbon.
β(1→4) is the lactose and cellulose bond. The glucose C1 bond here points down, and the O does not reach C4 of fructose.
The α,β part fits, but check the fructose end: the O joins fructose at its anomeric carbon, which is not C4.

q: Which polysaccharide is built from the same kind of glycosidic bond as the disaccharide shown?
h: Identify the bond: which carbons, and does the C1 bond point up (β) or down (α)?
w: The C1 bond of the left glucose points up, and the O joins it to C4: a β(1→4) bond (this disaccharide is cellobiose, released when cellulose is partly hydrolyzed). Cellulose is a chain of β(1→4) glucose. Amylose uses α(1→4); glycogen and amylopectin add α(1→6) branches.
x: Amylose uses α(1→4) bonds, with the C1 bond pointing down. In this drawing the C1 bond points up.
Glycogen has α linkages, with α(1→6) branches. The C1 bond in this drawing points up, which is not α.
Amylopectin has α(1→4) chains with α(1→6) branches. The C1 bond in this drawing points up, which is not α.

q: Is the disaccharide shown (sucrose) a reducing sugar?
c: No: both anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond
Yes: the glucose ring has a free hemiacetal –OH at C1
Yes: fructose is a ketose, and every ketose is reducing
No: a disaccharide can never be a reducing sugar
h: A reducing sugar needs one anomeric carbon that still has a free –OH (a hemiacetal that can open to C=O).
w: The bridging O uses C1 of glucose and C2 of fructose, the two anomeric carbons. Neither ring has a free hemiacetal, so neither can open, and sucrose gives a negative Benedict's test. Maltose and lactose are disaccharides that are reducing.
x: Glucose C1 is the carbon bonded to the bridging O, so it has no free hemiacetal –OH.
Not every ketose disaccharide is reducing; the question is whether an anomeric carbon still has a free –OH. Here fructose C2 is in the glycosidic bond.
"No" is right, but the reason is not: maltose and lactose are disaccharides that are reducing. Look at what is special about this glycosidic bond.

q: Maltose (shown) gives a positive Benedict's test. Which labeled carbon is responsible?
h: Look for an anomeric carbon (bonded to a ring O) that still has a free –OH instead of the bridging O.
w: Carbon a is C1 of the right glucose: it is bonded to the ring O and a free –OH, a hemiacetal that can open to an aldehyde and reduce Cu2+. Carbon b is the other anomeric carbon, but it is locked in the α(1→4) glycosidic bond (an acetal). Carbons c and d (C2 and C3) are not anomeric.
x: Carbon b is an anomeric carbon, but it is locked in the α(1→4) glycosidic bond as an acetal, so its ring cannot open.
Carbon c is C2 of a ring; it is not bonded to the ring oxygen, so it is not anomeric.
Carbon d is C3 of a ring, carrying only H and –OH. A reducing sugar needs a free hemiacetal carbon.

q: The disaccharide shown is completely hydrolyzed. Which two monosaccharides form?
h: Compare the left ring with glucose at C4. Hydrolysis just adds water across the glycosidic bond.
w: Both rings are six-membered aldohexoses. The right ring matches glucose; the left ring has its C4 –OH up, which makes it galactose. Adding H2O across the β(1→4) bond gives galactose + glucose. This disaccharide is lactose; people with lactose intolerance lack lactase, the enzyme for this step.
x: Compare the left ring with glucose at C4: its C4 –OH points up, while glucose's points down. So the two rings are not both glucose.
Fructose would appear as a five-membered ring. Both rings here are six-membered aldose rings.
Fructose would appear as a five-membered ring with a CH<sub>2</sub>OH on its anomeric carbon. Both rings here are six-membered aldoses.

q: Which Haworth projection shows α-D-galactopyranose?
h: α: C1 –OH down. Galactose differs from glucose only at C4 (–OH up).
w: α-D-galactopyranose has its anomeric (C1) –OH down and its C4 –OH up: structure II. The β form has C1 –OH up, α-glucose has C4 –OH down, and α-mannose differs at C2.
x: Structure III has its C1 –OH pointing up, which is β for a D-sugar.
Structure IV has its C4 –OH pointing down, as in glucose. Galactose differs from glucose at C4.
Structure I has its C2 –OH pointing up, which makes it mannose. Galactose differs from glucose at C4, not C2.

q: Four small biological molecules are drawn. Which one is a carbohydrate (a monosaccharide)?
h: A monosaccharide is a polyhydroxy aldehyde or ketone: look for a C=O (aldehyde or ketone) plus –OH on the other carbons.
w: Structure A is glyceraldehyde: an aldehyde carbon (–CHO) and an –OH on each remaining carbon, so it is an aldotriose. Glycerol has three –OH groups but no carbonyl (it is a sugar alcohol, not a sugar); lactic acid has a carboxylic acid, not an aldehyde or ketone; alanine has an amino group and a carboxyl group, so it is an amino acid.
x: B is glycerol: three –OH groups but no C=O. Without an aldehyde or ketone it is a sugar alcohol, not a sugar.
C is lactic acid. Its C=O is part of a carboxylic acid (–COOH), not an aldehyde or ketone.
D is alanine, an amino acid: it has an –NH<sub>2</sub> group and a –COOH group, and no polyhydroxy chain.

q: A biological polymer is hydrolyzed by dilute acid and gives only glucose. The bonds that held the monomers together are best described as which functional group?
h: Think about what forms when the hemiacetal –OH of one sugar ring reacts with an –OH of the next sugar.
w: A polymer of glucose is a polysaccharide (starch, glycogen or cellulose). Each glycosidic bond forms when the hemiacetal carbon of one glucose bonds through oxygen to an –OH of the next unit, giving an acetal (two –OR groups on one carbon). Esters link fatty acids in lipids, amides link amino acids in proteins and phosphodiesters link nucleotides.
x: Ester linkages join fatty acids to glycerol in fats. A polymer that gives only glucose is linked through sugar–O–sugar bonds.
Amide (peptide) bonds join amino acids in proteins. Hydrolysis here gives only glucose, not amino acids.
Phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides in DNA and RNA. Hydrolysis here gives only glucose, with no phosphate.

q: D-Arabinose, an aldopentose found in plant gums, is drawn at the top. Which of structures I–IV is the enantiomer (mirror image) of D-arabinose?
h: An enantiomer is the complete mirror image: every chiral carbon must have its H and OH swapped, not just one of them.
w: The mirror image of D-arabinose reverses all three chiral carbons: C2 right, C3 left, C4 left, which is structure I (L-arabinose). Structure III swaps only C4, so it is L but not the mirror image (a diastereomer); II (D-ribose) differs at only one carbon (an epimer) and IV (D-xylose) at two.
x: Structure II is right, right, right: D-ribose. It differs from D-arabinose at just one carbon (C2), so it is an epimer, not a mirror image.
Structure III reverses only C4 (left, right, left). It is an L-sugar, but a mirror image must reverse every chiral carbon.
Structure IV (right, left, right) differs from D-arabinose at C2 and C3 but not C4. It is still a D-sugar, so not the mirror image.

q: Glucose gives a positive Benedict's test (a reducing sugar) but sucrose does not. Which structural feature makes glucose a reducing sugar?
c: Its ring can open to a free aldehyde (hemiacetal carbon not locked in a glycosidic bond)
It has five –OH groups that are easily oxidized
Its ring oxygen can accept electrons from Cu<sup>2+</sup>
It contains an acetal carbon that is oxidized to a carboxylic acid
h: Benedict's reagent oxidizes aldehydes. Which carbon of glucose can become an aldehyde in solution, and why can't sucrose do the same?
w: In solution the cyclic hemiacetal of glucose opens to the free aldehyde, which Cu2+ oxidizes to a carboxylate (red Cu2O forms), so a free hemiacetal/aldehyde makes a sugar reducing. In sucrose both anomeric carbons are tied up as an acetal and a ketal, so no aldehyde can form. The alcohol –OH groups are not oxidized by Benedict's reagent.
x: The alcohol –OH groups are not oxidized by Benedict's reagent, and sucrose has many –OH groups too but tests negative.
The ring oxygen is not what reacts with Cu<sup>2+</sup>; sucrose has ring oxygens too and tests negative. Think about what the ring can open into.
An acetal carbon is locked and cannot open, which is why sucrose is non-reducing. Glucose on its own has no acetal carbon.

q: In its five-membered ring form, fructose has an –OH group and the ring oxygen both attached to carbon 2, which also bears two carbon groups. What functional group is at C2?
h: C2 of fructose is a ketone carbon in the open chain. What forms when an –OH adds to a ketone?
w: When the C5 –OH adds to the C2 ketone, the carbon ends up with –OH, –OR (the ring O) and two carbon substituents: a hemiketal. A hemiacetal would have an H on that carbon (from an aldose such as glucose); a ketal needs two –OR groups and forms only when the sugar makes a glycosidic bond.
x: A hemiacetal has an H on that carbon and comes from an aldehyde. Here C2 has two carbon groups because it came from a ketone.
A ketal has two –OR groups on the carbon. Here C2 still has one free –OH.
A ketone has a C=O. Once the ring closes, C2 no longer has a double bond to oxygen.

q: Each row of the table names a glucose polysaccharide and describes its linkages, branching and digestibility. Which row describes its polysaccharide correctly?
h: All four are glucose polymers. Sort them by α or β linkages, branching, and whether human enzymes can digest them.
w: Glycogen is the highly branched α(1→4)/α(1→6) glucose polymer that animals store in liver and muscle, so row II is correct. Row I is wrong because cellulose is β(1→4) and not digestible by humans; row III is wrong because amylose is unbranched; row IV is wrong because amylopectin is a plant starch, not a fructose polymer.

x: Row I is wrong about cellulose: cellulose has β(1→4) linkages, which human amylase cannot digest.
Row III is wrong about amylose: amylose has α(1→4) linkages and is unbranched.
Row IV is wrong about amylopectin: it is a branched glucose polymer in plant starch, not a fructose polymer in muscle.

q: A disaccharide is hydrolyzed to two D-glucose molecules. Benedict's test on the intact disaccharide is positive, and the enzyme that digests it in humans is maltase, not lactase or cellulase. Which linkage joins the two rings?
c: α(1→4), with one free hemiacetal carbon
β(1→4), with one free hemiacetal carbon
α,β(1→2), with no free hemiacetal carbon
α(1→6), with the two anomeric carbons used
h: Positive Benedict's test → a hemiacetal is still free. Maltase digests one specific kind of glucose–glucose bond.
w: Maltose is the glucose–glucose disaccharide hydrolyzed by maltase, joined α(1→4); its second ring keeps a free hemiacetal at C1, which opens to an aldehyde and reduces Cu2+. A β(1→4) glucose pair is cellobiose (from cellulose, not digestible); α,β(1→2) is sucrose, which is non-reducing because both anomeric carbons are used.
x: A β(1→4) glucose pair is cellobiose, from cellulose. Maltase does not break β bonds, and humans cannot digest them.
α,β(1→2) uses both anomeric carbons, as in sucrose, so it would test negative with Benedict's. This sugar tests positive and has no fructose.
If both anomeric carbons were used, no hemiacetal would be free and Benedict's test would be negative. Also, α(1→6) is the branch-point link, not maltose's.
